When a Child Death Occurs
Funeral Services In Calgary, Alberta
McInnis & Holloway has been one of Calgary and southern Alberta’s most respected funeral homes since 1903.
Our focus has always been on providing sympathetic assistance to families at a time of grief. We do that through highly trained and professional staff, and by delivering quality programs and funeral services. Many of our funeral services are unique in ​Calgary – we believe it’s the special things that make the grief process a little easier for families.
When the death of a child occurs, the loss, whether it's sudden or expected, is a deeply profound event. Amidst overwhelming emotions, even the simplest decisions can seem challenging. This section is dedicated to providing guidance in the immediate hours and days following the passing of a child.
What Happens Next
We want you to know that you are not alone, and we are here to assist.
At McInnis & Holloway, we are here to support you at every step. Planning a burial or cremation will be just one of many necessary steps, but we have the resources and dedicated funeral staff to assist you throughout this journey.
The following provided supporting materials are tailored to help you cope with your specific loss, whether it's related to stillbirths, infants, or the loss of a youth.
Click on the above image to view the digital version of these meaningful and helpful booklets. The "When a Child Dies" resources are readily available here on our website (digitally) or in person at any of our 11 locations at no cost for families.
What Happens Next
During this challenging time, we are committed to assisting you in navigating the funeral planning process with care and understanding. Our dedicated staff is available at our multiple locations, offering support in person, online, and over the phone. This ensures convenient access across our 11 locations throughout the city and surrounding areas whenever you are ready to begin the process of saying goodbye.
In these challenging times, we understand that leaving the house or hospital may not always be possible, especially when coping with the loss of a loved one. We want to offer our sincere condolences during this difficult period and provide support tailored to your needs.
If your family prefers to make arrangements entirely online, we have created an Online Cremation service to allow you to manage everything from the comfort of your home. Please use the following link to access the platform: Click Here
At McInnis & Holloway, we recognize that the loss of a child is an unimaginably difficult experience. To alleviate any additional stress, we firmly believe that financial concerns should not be a burden for families during such emotional times. In most cases, the total costs associated with cremation or burial services from McInnis & Holloway are zero dollars.
Our commitment is to provide compassionate and understanding support as you navigate these sensitive decisions. If you have any questions or require assistance, please don't hesitate to reach out to us. Our team is here for you every step of the way.
Wishing you strength and solace.
Sources Of Additional Help
Websites: 
A website recommended by both a perinatal professional and parents grieving miscarriage or later child loss is www.silentgrief.com. 
Share Pregnancy & Infant Loss Support Inc., www.nationalshare.org. 
The National Catholic Ministry to the Bereaved, www.griefwork.org
Books:
Empty Cradle, Broken Heart: Surviving the Death of Your Baby by Deborah L. Davis, Ph.D., Golden, Colorado, Fulcrum Publishing, 1996
Free to grieve: Healing and Encouragement for Those Who Have Suffered Miscarriage and Stillbirth by Maureen Rank, Minneapolis, Bethany House, 1985
Miscarriage after Infertility: A Woman’s Guide to Coping by Margaret Comerford Freda, R.N. and Carrie F. Semelsberger, R.N., Minneapolis, Fairview Press, 2023
Healing a Parent’s Grieving Heart: 100 Practical Ideas after Your Child Dies by Alan D. Wolfelt, Ph.D., Fort Collins, Colorado, Companion Press, 2002
Care Notes: Mourning a Miscarriage by Michaelene and Linus Mundy
Handling the Heartbreak when a Baby Dies by Jane Marie Lamb, O.S.F.; St. Meinrad, Indiana Abbey Press

# Sending Human and Cremated Remains

##### Transportation Guidelines From The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA)

McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes is an accredited Approved Air Cargo Known Consignor with trained and knowledgeable staff able to guide your family through this entire process.  

#### Traveling With Cremated Remains

We realize how difficult it is to lose a loved one, but knowing and planning to meet required conditions ahead of time can help you avoid disappointment at the airport. 

You may bring cremated remains in a cremation container or urn on the plane with you, but first it must pass through the X-ray.

*   It must be made of a material that allows the X-ray to clearly scan its contents.
*   It must pass security screening. Documentation from a funeral home does not provide an exemption to this requirement.
*   Screening officers are not permitted to open a cremation container, and they will not inspect the contents if you open it yourself.
*   It cannot be placed in checked baggage if it has been X-rayed at pre-board screening and its contents could not be determined.

_**Some airlines do not allow cremated remains in checked baggage, so please check with your airline first to learn about possible restrictions.**_

#### Before Going To The Airport:

*   Ask your funeral director about temporary containers for transportation purposes. These containers are more likely to pass through security.
*   You can also bring your empty permanent container with you and arrange for a funeral home at your destination to transfer the container contents.
*   Due to differences in thickness, shape and material, some cremation containers are more likely to pass through security screening.

**Most likely to be permitted:**

*   Lightweight Stone or other porous material
*   Cloth or biodegradable/paper containers
*   Plastic/resin (if not too thick)
*   Wood

**Least likely to be permitted:**  

*   Dense stone (e.g., marble, granite)
*   Metal
*   Ceramic (depends on glaze/thickness, often problematic)
*   Cardboard (sometimes allowed, but can vary-lightweight temporary containers are usually fine)

#### Options At The Airport

If your container does not pass pre-board screening for carry-on baggage, you may:

*   Leave the container with a friend or family member who is not travelling and still at the airport;
*   Ask your airline representative to re-book you on a later flight, allowing you time to make other arrangements; or
*   Ship the container via mail, cargo or courier. Please keep in mind that shipping options vary at airports.
*   Screening officers are not permitted to open a cremation container, and they will not inspect the contents if you open it yourself, unless it is empty.
*   It cannot be placed in checked baggage if it has been x-rayed at pre-board screening and did not pass security.

Cremation container and documentation requirements when travelling can vary, depending on your destination. If you are travelling internationally, we suggest you contact the embassy for the country of your destination before you fly to determine their specific requirements concerning the transport of cremated remains.

#### Repatriation/Flying with Cremated Remains (Urn) to U.S.A.

*   Consulate Involvement? NO
*   Funeral Director Statement of Death or Official Death Certificate
*   Certificate of Cremation
*   Burial Permit
*   Declaration of Contents from Funeral Home
*   If flying with the cremated remains, an approved urn when going through security or a temporary plastic urn

##### Repatriation of Human Remains (Casket) to U.S.A. (flying or driving)

*   Consulate Involvement? NO
*   Documentation required:
*   Funeral Director Statement of Death or Official Death Certificate
*   Coroners’ out of Province Certificate (which will list the cause of death)
*   Burial Permit
*   Letter from Public Health Office indicating no communicable disease
*   Letter of Embalming from Funeral Home & Declaration of Contents
*   Copy of passport 

###### Consulates/Embassies of U.S.A.

**US Consulate in Calgary**

615 Macleod Trail SE  
Rocky Mountain Plaza Building  
Calgary, AB T2G 2M1  
403-266-8962; CalgaryPD@state.gov

#### Shipping Human Remains FAQ

Can The Family Fly On The Same Flight As The Deceased?  

Unfortunately this is not always possible. The flights that are used to coordinate transporting human remains are not always commercial flights and those that are commercial flights may change under the discretion of the airlines.

Can Additional Items (Such As Mementos) Be Shipped In The Casket Or Urn?  

No. Additional items other than the necessary paperwork and the clothing articles worn by the deceased may not accompany the shipment.  

Does Clothing Have To Be Provided?  

Our staff will provide cloth shrouding in the event that the family is unable to, or wishes not to provide clothing (for spiritual or cultural reasons, for example).  

Can A Service Or Visitation Be Held In Canada Before The Shipment Proceeds?

Absolutely. Additional costs apply, but it is a common request.

How much does a casket weigh?

There are no alternatives for shipping a body to another country. However, some countries allow family members to travel with cremated remains into the country as long as they carry the pertinent documentation with them. The family must note that if they are travelling on a commercial flight with the remains, they should declare the urn as carry on and present the airline staff with the following:  

*   Proof of Death Certificate
*   Certificate of Cremation
*   Letter of Contents (indicating the specified container holding the remains)
*   Certified Copy of the Medical Certificate Form 16 (if required by the receiving country)

_For travel tips and a complete listing of all permitted and non-permitted items, please visit www.catsa.gc.ca/whatcanIbring._

Scattering Cremated Remains | McInnis & Holloway
Choosing where and how to scatter cremated remains can be a deeply personal decision, and we are here to help you plan a respectful and meaningful tribute. 
Alberta Parks supports scattering of cremated remains for personal, spiritual, and/or religious purposes. The process of scattering cremated remains in these locations should consider the impact to the public and the environment. 
Alberta Parks recommends the following guidance:

Cremated remains should be completely pulverized before scattering. No ferrous or non-ferrous metal products, metal identification disk, teeth, bone fragments or remnants recognizable as human remains should be visible.
Cremated remains should be fully dispersed such that no obvious remnants of scattering remain.
Only biodegradable vessels may be used when scattering cremated remains. No other container, urn, or ancillary objects, including but not limited to markers, plants, or decorations, may be deposited with the scattered remains. This requirement reduces the potential for unintended distribution of invasive objects or species into the environment.
Cremated remains should be scattered to avoid developed areas or high public activity areas.
Cremated remains should be scattered to avoid the depositing of high concentrations in one location.
If a ceremony is to take place, it should not impede the enjoyment of others in a public setting.
Care should be taken to ensure that cremated remains are not scattered near drinking water intakes or recreational water activities, such as swimming areas.
In some locations and trails, group size limits may apply due to ecological sensitivities. Please note that for large groups wishing to hold ceremonies in a park or protected area, a special event permit may be required.
Source: Alberta Parks
Scattering Ashes
The scattering of cremated remains in Alberta may occur on lands regulated by the province of Alberta (public land), including within public waters, in accordance with Environment and Protected Areas’ Scattering of Cremated Remains in Alberta (Guidelines), and with provincial laws and regulations governing these areas, including the Public Lands Act, the Public Lands Administrative Regulation, the Water Act and the Water Regulations.
Where distribution of cremated remains on vacant public land is undertaken according to Environment and Protected Areas’ Scattering of Cremated Remains in Alberta (Guidelines), no permission is required. If distribution is occurring on public land under disposition, permission for access to this land through the disposition holder should be sought.
There may be additional requirements in areas of Alberta regulated by Environment and Protected Areas.
Please contact Environment and Protected Areas for information on permits, group size restrictions and other requirements for Special Events.
For information on scattering ashes in a National Park, please contact Parks Canada.
When scattering ashes within municipal or privately held lands, you must obtain permission from the landowner for access and for scattering of the cremated remains.
Source: Cemeteries Act and Regulations

Payment Options

Available Payment Methods
At McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home Ltd., we are committed to offering families flexible, respectful, and efficient payment solutions. Our options support timely settlement of accounts, ensuring funeral services can proceed without delay. Please note that services such as cremation, burial, or repatriation may be delayed or prevented without prior payment.
1. E-Transfer
Send payment via your financial institution's online banking:
Select Interac e-Transfer
Send to: mhaccounting@mhfh.com
McInnis & Holloway is registered for Interac Autodeposit, so no security question is needed
Your bank will confirm once funds are deposited
2. Credit/Debit Card
Visa, MasterCard, and debit cards are accepted. Payments can be made at the time of arrangements or online at mhfh.com under "Make a Payment." Online payment and all payments processed without the card present will incur an additional 2.4% card not present credit card processing fee applied by the online merchant. Additional services or disbursements will be included on the final invoice.
3. Cheque
Personal or certified cheques are accepted at the time of arrangements. Make cheques payable to McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home Ltd. A final invoice will reflect any additional charges.
4. Cash
Cash must be paid in full at the time of arrangements. Additional charges will be reflected in a final invoice if needed.
5. Insurance Proceeds
If the Deceased had life insurance, we can help request funds directly from the provider. Signed authorization forms may be required.
Processing may take time
If delayed, an alternate form of payment may be needed to avoid service delays
6. Direct Payment from the Estate
Funeral expenses can be paid directly from the Deceased's bank account or estate. Alberta law allows financial institutions to release funds for funeral costs before probate when sufficient assets exist.
We provide a letter to support this process, which can be presented to the bank with the death certificate and funeral account.
7. Treasured Memories Community Funding
Raise funds for families in need of assistance with a funeral bill and other unexpected expenses.
Questions?
Please speak with your funeral director if you have questions or need assistance selecting the best payment method.

# Payment Options

  

## Available Payment Methods

At McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home Ltd., we are committed to offering families flexible, respectful, and efficient payment solutions. Our options support timely settlement of accounts, ensuring funeral services can proceed without delay. Please note that services such as cremation, burial, or repatriation may be delayed or prevented without prior payment.

### 1\. E-Transfer

Send payment via your financial institution's online banking:

*   Select Interac e-Transfer
*   Send to: [mhaccounting@mhfh.com](mailto:mhaccounting@mhfh.com)
*   McInnis & Holloway is registered for **Interac Autodeposit**, so no security question is needed
*   Your bank will confirm once funds are deposited

### 2\. Credit/Debit Card

Visa, MasterCard, and debit cards are accepted. Payments can be made at the time of arrangements or online at mhfh.com under "Make a Payment." **Online payment and all payments processed without the card present will incur an additional 2.4% card not present credit card processing fee applied by the online merchant.** Additional services or disbursements will be included on the final invoice.

### 3\. Cheque

Personal or certified cheques are accepted at the time of arrangements. Make cheques payable to **McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home Ltd.** A final invoice will reflect any additional charges.

### 4\. Cash

Cash must be paid in full at the time of arrangements. Additional charges will be reflected in a final invoice if needed.

### 5\. Insurance Proceeds

If the Deceased had life insurance, we can help request funds directly from the provider. Signed authorization forms may be required.

*   Processing may take time
*   If delayed, an alternate form of payment may be needed to avoid service delays

### 6\. Direct Payment from the Estate

Funeral expenses can be paid directly from the Deceased's bank account or estate. Alberta law allows financial institutions to release funds for funeral costs before probate when sufficient assets exist.

We provide a letter to support this process, which can be presented to the bank with the death certificate and funeral account.

### 7\. Treasured Memories Community Funding

Raise funds for families in need of assistance with a funeral bill and other unexpected expenses.

* * *

## Questions?

Please speak with your funeral director if you have questions or need assistance selecting the best payment method.

McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home Ltd. is Proud to be the recipient of the 2024 Consumer Choice Award for Business Excellence, having won the prestigious honor 10 consecutive times.
Being selected to be on the consumer survey for the Consumer Choice Award is an honor, and winning the award is an achievement that few businesses will experience. McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home has been able to accomplish this for 10 consecutive years, as the Consumers’ Choice Award winner in Funeral Homes in Calgary.
The loss of a loved one is a difficult time for everyone. Working with a funeral home that offers trusted, compassionate and professional care will make a difficult time much less stressful. McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home has a proven record of customer service, products and a variety of facilities and service options to meet your specific requirements. This family owned funeral home is experienced in working with specific religious and ethnic requirements for funeral arrangements, which can simplify the planning and organization of the funeral itself.

The management team of Ernie Hagel, his son Jeff Hagel, Janine Altamirano and the licensed professional staff are dedicated to assisting families in very difficult times. The company prides itself on professionalism, empathy and quality service with compassion.
McInnis & Holloway Funeral Home has ten locations in Calgary, Cochrane & Airdrie and our highly professional staff are available 24 hours a day to provide service and information and together we were voted best of the Funeral Home in Calgary as voted by Calgarians.
The Consumer Choice Award are unique to Canada and the United States. They allow the actual consumers in the marketplace to select businesses by category that are the best in all aspects of customer service, sales and product and service selection. This prestigious award helps future customers identify a great business within the community and allows businesses to also recognize other companies in the area that are outstanding in their services and products.

It is the goal of the Consumer Choice Awards to spotlight only the best representations of business excellence in each market, like McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. To accomplish this, they avoid the influences of third parties like industry insiders and advocate groups, allow every person no more than one vote, and leave all results to the independent research firm.
The process of surveying each community is done following a specific set of criteria to learn which companies are the favorites in categories like best funeral home in Calgary & surrounding area. Once the leading companies are discovered, a majority vote takes place to announce the winners. There is always a great deal of competition between local businesses for the award, which makes winning far from easy. Obituary information for Glen Robert Richardson
June 26, 1939 – Calgary, Alberta
July 19, 2026 – Calgary, Alberta
It is with profound sadness that we announce the sudden passing of Glen (GR) Richardson after complications from a fall at his home.
Glen spent his last day doing exactly what he liked: breakfast with his cousins, then on to a car show with a friend. For this, his family will always be grateful.
The son of Lawrence and Violet Richardson, Glen spent his childhood in Nanton and Vulcan, AB, fueling countless stories of adventure and mischief, captivating audiences throughout his life. From the start, he was a connector of people and was proud that he remained in contact with his elementary school friends.
The Richardsons moved to Lethbridge, AB, where Glen briefly attended the Lethbridge Collegiate Institute before deciding that the traditional classroom setting was not the place for him. His love of vehicles and natural aptitude for mechanics led him to Fleming Motors, where he applied to become a Service Technician. Recognizing Glen's gift with people, management hired him to work at the service desk instead. Within a few weeks, he was named the youngest Service Manager in Canada.
Shortly afterward, Glen was fortunate enough to meet and marry local beauty, Jeanette Romanchuk, with whom he celebrated 65 years of matrimony in April of this year.
After welcoming three children, Todd, Kari and David, the family moved to Calgary, AB, where he made a name for himself in the city, opening several automotive-related businesses in the area, including The Used Car Chalet, 5 Star Motor Homes, Glen Richardson Pontiac Buick, culminating in the opening of Charlesglen Toyota with partners Gordon and Glen Rumpel in 1988.
As Dealer and Managing Partner, Glen's unmatched work ethic and belief that he was in the “people business” created the culture for the successful, customer-focused business it remains today. He was proud that his life's philosophy of “it doesn't matter who's right, it's what's right that counts” is the guiding principle by which the dealerships in which he had partnerships, including Lexus of Royal Oak and 5th Avenue Volkswagen, are managed.
Glen served as President of the Calgary Motor Dealers Association from 1998 to 1999. In 2004, he was awarded the Motor Dealers Association of Alberta Dealer of Excellence Award in recognition of his outstanding leadership, integrity, and contributions to the industry.
Glen had an innate ability to make people feel valued, whether it was someone he had known his whole life or a stranger he met in an elevator. He liked nothing more than to make his rounds at the dealerships and greet the team members with his broad, handsome grin, asking them to share a little about themselves. Some would say it was his superpower to connect with others.
His kindness and generosity of spirit went well beyond the business world and, as a proud Rotarian of 49 years, he lived by the mantra, “Service Above Self.” Glen joined Rotary South, now the Rotary Club of Calgary at Stampede Park, serving as President from 2001 to 2002. He took pride in his almost perfect record of attendance and spent countless volunteer hours serving on committees and working late-night shifts selling Dream Home tickets as recently as July. Delighted to be in the company of children, Glen's most recent focus was on the annual Rotary Kids at Heart Golf Tournament, supporting child-focused charities in Calgary. Glen's commitment to Rotary extended to the Sunrise Club of Scottsdale, where he and Jeanette spent their winters, attending weekly meetings and volunteering at their annual Special Day for Special Kids Picnic.
In 2022, Glen was recognized for his commitment to volunteerism and giving back to society with the honour of receiving the Queen Elizabeth II Platinum Jubilee Medal (Alberta).
Glen lived a car-centric life from early on. At the age of twelve, he obtained his first vehicle, a 1928 coupe. In his late teens, Glen joined “The Govners Car Club” in Lethbridge, AB, customizing classic cars and building hot rods. A testament to his skills, his 1952 Chev was featured in the U.S. annual publication “Custom Cars” in 1961. Glen was a well-known attendee at local car auctions and, after a lifetime of enjoyment amassing an extensive collection, he sold them at Mecum Auction in Glendale, AZ, in 2020, donating the proceeds to charity.
As much as his business interests, volunteerism, and classic car collecting provided Glen with a full and rewarding life, nothing brought him more pride and enjoyment than being with his family. Having recently returned from a family holiday, they are eternally grateful for the memories made in his loving presence.
Those left behind to forever miss the light of his love are his beloved wife, Jeanette; his son, Todd (Natasha) Richardson; his grandchildren, Alex Richardson, Zoe Richardson, and Julia Richardson (Austin Masse); daughter Kari (Sean) Meggs; his grandchildren, Bryanna Meggs (Matt Estabillo) and Denver Meggs; his daughter-in-law, Treasure Richardson; his granddaughter, Jade McKitrick (Connor); his great-grandchild Xander, and grandson Kai MacMillen-Skead. Glen's sisters, Norma Lebsack and Ruby Blackwood (Gerry); a large extended family, and a loving group of friends share in the deep grief of his passing.
Providing some peace as we mourn our insurmountable loss here on Earth, the family takes comfort in knowing Glen is reunited with his beloved son David, who has been intensely missed since August of 2015.
The old adage, “To know him is to love him,” was never more appropriate than when applied to Glen. We invite all who were touched by Glen's kindness, leadership, compassion for others, and genuine love of people to join us as we celebrate his remarkable life.
A Service of Remembrance will be held in the Champion’s Ballroom of the BMO Centre (1912 Flores Ladue Parade SE, Calgary, AB), on Friday, September 11, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. Reception to follow in the Champion’s Ballroom.
To park on the day of the service, enter the area from the south via 25th Ave. S.E. and follow Stampede Trail, turning left onto Corral Trail/Flores LaDue Parade. Lot 3 would be best for parking. Use the Culture and Entertainment District Access Map for the most up-to-date impacts to roads, sidewalks, and intersections: https://www.cedistrict.com/access-map.
You can also enter from the north on Stampede Trail, then turn right onto Corral Trail/Flores LaDue Parade or proceed to Lot 3.
The drop-off zones are by Spirit of Water and then between the canopy and the Saddledome.
Please enter through the door beside Lammles.
To commemorate Glen's love for classic cars, the family requests that those in attendance with access to a classic vehicle drive it to the service in his honour, as Glen did love a good car show! Please let us know if you will be participating by emailing Rememberinggr@gmail.com.
Family and friends who are unable to attend in person are invited to join Mr. Richardson’s service streamed live (see link below) on the day of the service. For those who are unable to view live, a recording of the service will be posted.
In lieu of flowers and to honour Glen's commitment to giving back, we ask that donations in his name be made to the registered charity the Rotary Club of Calgary at Stampede Park by e-transferring to donations@rotarycs.org or through CanadaHelps using the link: https://www.canadahelps.org/en/charities/Rotary-club-of-Calgary-at-Stampede-Park-community-service-fund/. In either case, please indicate that the gift is in honour of Glen Richardson.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Glen’s family here.
In living memory of Glen Richardson, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Crowfoot, 82 Crowfoot Circle NW, Calgary, AB T3G 2T3, Telephone: 403-241-0044.

Obituary information for Angela Kwai Ying Yuen Yip
October 9, 1931 – Hong Kong, China
July 18, 2026 – Calgary, Alberta
Angela Yuen passed away peacefully, surrounded by her loving family, on Saturday, July 18, 2026, at the age of 94.
Angela was born in Hong Kong, China, on October 9, 1931, and moved to Calgary, AB, in 1990.
She graduated from the United College in Hong Kong with a degree in Fine Arts and Languages. She dedicated her life to teaching primary school children until her retirement.
Angela married Dominic Yuen, and together they had four children.
She was an active member of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church (OLPH) and volunteered countless hours at the St. Paul’s Pre-school in Calgary.
Angela accomplished much throughout her life and was particularly proud of educating thousands of young children and keeping her family together.
She cherished family gatherings, especially sharing meals during major Chinese and Canadian holidays, where she would often hand out traditional red pockets as symbols of blessing and good fortune. She will be most remembered for her beautiful smile and love of family.
Angela is survived and lovingly remembered by her children, Anne Yuen, Fatima Yuen, Tony Yuen (Cindy Luk), and Francis Yuen (Paula McCoy); her grandchildren, Jenny Yuen and Johnny Yuen; and her granddogs, Bobby, Kaia, and the late Zoe.
She was predeceased by her husband, Dominic Yuen, and her sister, Anne Au-Yeung (Anthony Au-Yeung).
Those wishing to pay their respects may do so at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church (400 Edmonton Trail, Calgary, AB), on Friday, July 31, 2026, from 5:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend Vigil Prayers and Tributes at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church (400 Edmonton Trail, Calgary, AB), on Friday, July 31, 2026, at 6:00 p.m.
Funeral Mass will be celebrated at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church (400 Edmonton Trail, Calgary, AB), on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. Graveside Service to follow at Queen’s Park Cemetery (3219 4 St NW, Calgary, AB). Reception to follow at Phoenix Gate Chinese Cuisine (1518 Centre Street N, Calgary, AB).
In consideration of allergies, the family kindly requests that guests refrain from bringing fragrant flowers.
If friends so desire, in lieu of flowers, memorial tributes may be made directly to Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church, www.myolph.org, or to the Calgary Health Trust, www.calgaryhealthfoundation.ca.
The family wishes to send special thanks to Dr. Sandi Dumanski, Ms. Ellen Novak, Dr. Albert Kryski, Ms. Tracy French, Dr. John Poon, The Queen of China Club at OLPH, and the staff at Rockyview General Hospital and Agape Hospice for their love and compassion.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Angela’s family here.
In living memory of Angela Yuen, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Chapel of the Bells, 2720 Centre Street North, Calgary, AB T2E 2V6, Telephone: 403-276-2296.

She was predeceased by her husband, Dominic Yuen, and her sister, Anne Au-Yeung (Anthony Au-Yeung).

Those wishing to pay their respects may do so at Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church ([400 Edmonton Trail, Calgary, AB](https://maps.app.goo.gl/MxEhXz9T15uxwQoEA)), on Friday, July 31, 2026, from 5:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.

Obituary information for Marilyn Lundquist
February 1, 1940 – Didsbury, Alberta
July 18, 2026 – Calgary, Alberta
Marilyn Lundquist, beloved wife of the late Joseph Lundquist, of Calgary, AB, passed away on Saturday, July 18, 2026, at the age of 86 years.
Marilyn was born at the hospital in Didsbury, AB, on February 1, 1940, the youngest of six children and the only one to be born in a hospital. She grew up on a farm in the Carstairs, AB, area where she rode a horse to school as a young girl and gained a love for nature.
After high school, Marilyn attended the University of Alberta’s Calgary Campus where she attained her teaching certificate. She went on to teach Grade 1 and Grade 2 in Carstairs, something that she enjoyed very much.
Marilyn met Joe when he rented a room above the garage from Marilyn’s parents while he was working on a local drilling rig. They were married in the St. Agnes Church in Carstairs on July 21, 1962.
Marilyn and Joe lived in Rainbow Lake, AB, Drayton Valley, AB, and Calgary, where they spent most of their years raising two children. She worked for the Calgary Catholic School Board in several distinct positions until her retirement.
In their retirement years, Marilyn and Joe spent time travelling throughout North America in their motorhome as well as travelling to Sweden and England to visit relatives and trace family history. Marilyn spent many long hours researching family genealogy at Carlisle Castle in the Lake District of England and assembled binders of her hard work to share with family.
Later in retirement, Marilyn and Joe had a condo on the water in Victoria, BC, where Marilyn loved to spend time walking, shopping, and talking to people. She spent a lot of happy days there and forged new friendships. Marilyn also cherished her time living on a wooded acreage in the Water Valley, AB, area where she built a nice community of good friends. Something she did wherever she would go.
Marilyn’s final years were spent living in her condo in Calgary, having coffee and conversation with friends or strangers at the local Starbucks. She spent a lot of her time with friends and enjoyed their company very much. Marilyn loved the weekly Sunday morning family breakfasts and the many weekends spent with Leslie, David, and Marla at Leslie’s acreage in the forest.
Marilyn loved her children fiercely, was a shoulder to lean on for many, and met everyone with love and empathy. She helped anyone in need, from family to strangers, with love and care to spare.
She lived life her way, with a smile, right to the end.
Marilyn will be lovingly remembered and missed by her daughter, Leslie Lundquist, of Calgary, AB; her son, David Lundquist (Marla Grossman) of Olds, AB; her brother, Bill Steckly of Didsbury, AB; her sister, Shirley Gingerich of Canby, Oregon; as well as a long list of nephews, nieces, great-nephews, great-nieces and many friends.
Marilyn was predeceased by her two infant children in 1965 and 1971; her parents, Alvin Steckly (1905-1972) and Lilly Steckly (née Taylor) (1901-1988); and her brothers, Floyd Steckly (1926-1926), David Steckly (1930-2017), and Dale Steckly (1928-2023).
A Celebration of Marilyn’s Life will be held at McInnis & Holloway (Crowfoot, 82 Crowfoot Circle NW, Calgary, AB), on Friday, August 7, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Reception to follow in the Hospitality Centre at the Funeral Home.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Marilyn’s family here.
In living memory of Marilyn Lundquist, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Crowfoot, 82 Crowfoot Circle NW, Calgary, AB T3G 2T3, Telephone: 403-241-0044.

Obituary information for Ha To 鄭志強 "Tommy" Trinh
November 11, 1950 – Saigon, Vietnam
July 18, 2026– Calgary, Alberta
It is with shattering heartbreak and pain that we announce the passing of our very beloved, honourable, and amazing husband and father, 鄭志強先生, Mr. Tommy (Ha To) Trinh, of Calgary, AB, Canada, on Saturday, July 18, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. He was 75 but looked like he was not a day over 60!
Dad was born in Saigon, Vietnam, on November 11, 1950, and was the youngest son of eleven children to 鄭九公 and 賴好.
Tommy was a known community figure during the 1980s and 90s in Calgary, AB. Providing support, experience, and friendship to small businesses and those within the Chinese and Vietnamese communities.
Dad learned and helped his brother-in-law run a printing business in Vietnam at the young age of seventeen. He brought his experience with him upon arriving in Canada and continued offering his knowledge to the printing industry for over 40 years. Dad proudly owned City Prints from 1999 to 2023 and even stayed on to be a consultant after new ownership.
Dad enjoyed nature, road trips to the mountains, rivers, lakes, waterfalls, and oceans. He enjoyed new innovations, gadgets and ensured he kept up with the pace of technology, graphic design programs, and AI!
Truthfully, Dad’s success was not in his print shop business, but in the very protected and tight-knit family he built. Tommy is survived by his wife, Phuong Hue Luu; and his daughters, Lily Trinh, Shirley Trinh, and Kelly Trinh. He is also survived by his sons-in-law, Dicky Lin, Jason Chang, and Ernesto Ascura; and his grandchildren, Kinley Marie Ascura, Nicholas KC Lin, Mia KH Lin, Kingston Mikah Ascura, and Hailey Chang; his older sister here in Canada, an older sister in Vietnam, and an older sister in China; along with many nieces and nephews around the world.
He was predeceased by his very beloved son, the late Johnson Trinh.
Dad always took pride in how he created a paradise in Canada for a dream family he had envisioned during his time in Vietnam—a war-stricken country that offered very little hope for the future. He took on a mission to crowdfund, lead and coordinate the building of a boat and took 300 people out of Vietnam into a refugee camp in Malaysia, where everyone then had the opportunity to apply for refugee status with first world countries, offering hope, opportunities, and a future.
As his children, we take true pride and glory to confirm that Dad indeed gave us a life of paradise in freedom, safety, and stability. We are immensely honoured to be Tommy’s children, family, and grandchildren.
Funeral Services will be held at McInnis & Holloway (Chapel of the Bells, 2720 Centre Street North, Calgary, AB), on Tuesday, July 28, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. The family asks that all attendees arrive prior to this time. A Memorial Graveside Service will follow at Mountain View Cemetery (Memorial Gardens, 1605 100 Street SE, Calgary, AB).
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Tommy’s family here.
In living memory of Tommy Trinh, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Chapel of the Bells, 2720 Centre Street North, Calgary, AB T2E 2V6, Telephone: 403-276-2296.

Obituary information for Georgie Poucette
November 10, 1938 – Mînî Thnî
July 18, 2026 – Calgary, Alberta
Georgie Poucette, of Mînî Thnî, AB, passed away in her sleep on Saturday, July 18, 2026, at the age of 87 years.
Born on November 10, 1938, Georgie lived a life defined by kindness, hard work, and love for her family.
Georgie was a kind soul; she was known for her warm heart and helping hands. She loved crafts, beading, cooking, and making dry meat – sharing what she made with family, friends, and anyone who needed it.
She found so much joy watching hockey, especially cheering on her grandchildren.
Ena was a survivor; she taught all of us always to be humble, to be kind to people, and to help whenever we could. Whether she was sitting with someone who needed to talk or for just a short visit and laugh. Making something with her hands or cooking bannock with her granddaughters, she did it with love and grace. It was important to Georgie to refer to those by their relation, not by name. She leaves behind a legacy of compassion that will live on in all of us.
“Always be kind and be ready to help.” She lived by those words every single day, and we will carry them with us always.
Georgie is lovingly remembered by her children, Lorraine, Marvin, and Vernon (Loretta) Abraham, Myrna, and Noreen Wesley-Beaver, Randall (Cynthia), Shirley, Harlen, Lenny, and Tracy Poucette, and Carrie Labelle; and daughters-in-law, Geraldine Twoyoungmen and Eleanor Smallboy; son-in-law Marvin Blackrabbit; siblings, Cassie Poucette, Annie Wesley, Ina Poucette, and Tina Poucette; friends, John Wesley and Charlie Abraham; 25 grandchildren, 73 great-grandchildren, and many nieces, nephews, and other family members who love her.
She was predeceased by her parents, John Sr. and Sara; and stepmother Jane; her husband Isaac Wesley-Beaver; her sons, Oliver Abraham and Peter Wesley-Beaver; daughter Colleen Wesley-Beaver; her grandchildren, Steven, Trey and Colton Abraham, Clarissa Wesley-Beaver, Kylie Cecil, and Darcy Beaver; brother John (Evelyn) Poucette Jr.; and her sisters, Mary Jane and Caroline Snow, and Margaret Lagrelle.
Wake Services will be held at the residence of Georgie Poucette (Mînî Thnî, AB) on Wednesday, July 22, 2026.
Funeral Services will be held at Mînî Thnî Gymnasium (Mînî Thnî, AB) on Friday, July 24, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Graveside Service to follow at Goodstoney Cemetery (Mînî Thnî, AB). Following the Graveside Service, friends and relatives are invited to join the family for a Traditional Feast at the Goodstoney Rodeo Centre (Mînî Thnî, AB).
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Georgie’s family here.
In living memory of Georgie Poucette, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Cochrane, 369 Railway Street, Cochrane, AB T4C 2E2, Telephone: 403-932-4740.

Obituary information for Richard (Rick) Gale Kane
August 24, 1948 – Calgary, Alberta
July 19, 2026 – Calgary, Alberta
LUCTOR ET EMERGO
(I Struggle And Emerge)
It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Richard "Rick" Kane on Sunday, July 19, 2026, at the age of 77.
Rick was the beloved only child of Hughie and Laura Kane. He spent most of his life in Calgary, AB, a city he was proud to call home.
He attended Notre Dame College in Wilcox, SK, an experience he often said was the best thing that ever happened to him. It was there that he formed many friendships that he treasured throughout his life.
Rick enjoyed a successful 37-year career with Topco Oilsite Products, where he became a partner on two occasions. The final years of his career were spent in Red Deer, AB, where Rick and Toby built many enduring friendships. This is where Rick continued to hone his horserace handicapping skills.
A passionate golfer, Rick was a founding member of Country Hills Golf Club. He also had a lifelong love of music, followed sports religiously, and was endlessly curious about history, current events, and politics. His remarkable memory and breadth of knowledge ensured he was always the person you wanted on your side for a game of trivia.
Rick was generous to a fault, blessed with a quick wit, and known for his sharp sense of humour and trademark sarcasm. He made people laugh with his dry observations and was always ready with the perfect comeback.
Together, Rick and Toby shared a love of travel and created countless cherished memories. Their adventures included river cruises, winters in Maui, and trips to Ireland, England, Scotland, and the Maritimes, as well as many happy months spent in Surprise, AZ. Family vacations were a treasured tradition, filled with laughter, unforgettable moments, and memories that will be cherished for years to come.
After spending four and a half years on hemodialysis, Rick received the extraordinary gift of a kidney transplant, giving him 27 more years of life and providing his family and friends with precious years they otherwise would not have had. A reminder to all to sign your donor card and give the gift of life. Throughout his life, he faced many health challenges, yet he did so with remarkable resilience and grace. He rarely complained, never surrendered to adversity, and met every obstacle with courage, determination, and quiet strength. Rick was, simply put, a fighter.
Rick leaves behind his beloved wife of 55 years, Toby (née Stapleton), his children, Chris (Jackie), Megan (Brad Shaback), and Tim (Amy); and his grandboys, Hayden Kane (Ryleigh), Noel Shaback, and Nate Shaback (Anika). He is also lovingly remembered by his extended family, including his special niece and nephews, and by many dear friends whose lives were enriched by his kindness, generosity, humour, and unwavering friendship.
The family extends its heartfelt gratitude to the doctors and nurses at Foothills Medical Centre for their compassionate care. Special thanks are owed to Rick's nephrologist, Dr. Kevin McLaughlin, and to his dedicated nurses, Pat and Sherry, whose exceptional care, support, and kindness over the years meant so much to him and his family.
A Celebration of Rick’s Life will be held at McInnis & Holloway (Crowfoot, 82 Crowfoot Circle NW, Calgary, AB), on Saturday, July 25, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. Reception to follow in the Hospitality Centre at the Funeral Home. Summer attire is suggested.
Rick will be deeply missed, lovingly remembered, and forever cherished by all who had the privilege of knowing him. If friends so desire, memorial tributes may be made directly to the Kidney Foundation of Canada, Southern Alberta Branch, www.kidney.ca, or to a charity of your choice.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared and viewed with Rick’s family here.
In living memory of Richard (Rick) Kane, a tree will be planted in the Ann & Sandy Cross Conservation Area by McInnis & Holloway Funeral Homes. Additional memorial trees will be planted through Canadian conservation and reforestation initiatives, as a result of memorial contributions. McInnis & Holloway, Crowfoot, 82 Crowfoot Circle NW, Calgary, AB T3G 2T3, Telephone: 403-241-0044.

Burial Services
In Calgary, Alberta

Cemetery Burial Types

Lawn cemetery: A lawn cemetery is where each grave is marked with a small commemorative plaque that is placed horizontally at the head of the grave at ground-level. Families can still be involved in the design and in choosing the information contained on the plaque, but in most cases the plaques are a standard design.
Mausoleum: A mausoleum is an external, free-standing building constructed as a monument enclosing the interment space or burial chamber of a deceased person or people. A mausoleum may be considered a type of tomb, or the tomb may be considered to be within the mausoleum.

Conventional markings, such as headstones, are generally replaced with a tree, bush, or the placement of a natural stone.
Burial FAQ
How much does the average funeral cost?
As a full service funeral home, we offer a wide variety of services and facilities with costs for a family ranging from approx. $4000.00 – $12,000.00, with an average of about $6000.00 – $8000.00.
Why do funerals cost so much? Can you explain what is involved in this cost?
It is estimated that there are 48.5 man hours required for a funeral service. This would include:
Securing a release and transfer from the place of death, embalming and sanitation of the deceased, cosmetology, hairdressing, dressing and casketing.
Funeral Director meets with the family to coordinate the funeral service and coordination of all details with respect to the cemetery or crematorium, clergy, casket, flowers and musicians.
Record keeping and clerical assistance, including completion and filing of all government forms, securing necessary permits and preparation and placement of obituaries.
Secretarial services for memorial book, service folders, statements of death and general inquiries regarding funeral service.
Arranging flowers for visitation and preparing viewing room and staff for visitation to meet and direct people.
Preparation and cleaning of motor vehicles for the funeral service.
Arranging flowers, casket and general set up for the funeral service.
Staffing for the funeral service and general cleanup of the facilities and equipment before and after the service.
Invoicing and general bookkeeping duties, as well as a visit by Family Care staff to assist with benefit applications, government forms, cancelling pensions, etc.
A factor that contributes to the cost of the funeral is the type of casket that is chosen, as well as flowers, obituaries, musicians and other service enhancements that are not included in our regular schedule of fees.
Can we have a green burial or cremation?
While there has not yet been a cemetery in Calgary that has been designated “true” green, there has been discussion about the possibility of one being started. McInnis and Holloway are able to provide a casket that does meet green requirements and can be used for either burial or cremation.
Click here for an informational video on green burial.
Why would we want to consider burial for our loved ones?
With burial the location of the cemetery gives the family a permanent place for them to memorialize the loss of their loved one and place to visit their family member.
How much does a casket weigh?
The weight of a casket will vary depending on the casket selected and the materials used in the construction of it. Caskets may range from 60 pounds but could be 200 pounds.
If the weight of a specific casket is needed we are able to have the manufacture provide the correct weight.
How long is the funeral service?
Although there is no set time for a funeral service the average length is approximately one hour.
The length of time will depend on how many people are speaking, the number of musical selections, the service being held in a church or another venue, whether communion is being served, tributes and readings.
Following the approximately one hour funeral service there is often a reception or gathering (with refreshments) allowing you time to meet and speak with the family. There may also be a procession to the graveside service.
When should we have the service?
When to have a service is often dependent on a number of factors. If the disposition is burial then arrangement for the cemetery plot will need to be considered and may dictate the day the grave can be open.
If cremation is to take place before the service then time is required to have the urn prepared and cremated remains placed inside.
Consideration needs to be given as to when family may be able to gather. Many families need to travel long distances and time is given for them to arrive. The facilities used for the services need to be arranged and coordinated with the family as to the dates they are considering.
The role of the Funeral Director is to help in the coordination of these various situations and circumstances.
Can we do a service in the evening or on the weekend?
Absolutely, an evening or weekend service can be accommodated. The availability of the venue, such as the funeral home chapel or reception centre, church, hall, clubs, etc., must first be secured before a date is confirmed.
Quite often having the ability and flexibility to have an evening or weekend service can greatly alleviate many concerns the family may have while planning their particular service.
There is a surcharge applicable for evening and weekend services and the Funeral Director will advise on those costs during the arrangements.
We don’t want a traditional funeral what else can we do?
There are many ways to pay tribute and honour your loved one's life and allow for a time for family and friends to show their support. It can be simple, elaborate, religious or contemporary.
These services can be in a church, funeral home, reception centre or community hall.
Does the Funeral have to happen right away?
No. Funeral services can be scheduled days or even weeks after a death, depending on your family’s wishes, cultural or religious considerations, and what works best for those involved.
Can you provide a Minister/Celebrant for the service if we do not have anyone to help us?
Yes, we have clergy and celebrants that we can contact that will facilitate a meaningful funeral service no matter what faith is followed or if you desire a more non-religious service.
My loved one was not a religious person, do I need a minister?
An ordained clergy person is not required to preside at funeral services nor does the presider need to be licensed in any manner.
An individual who feels a comfort level with public speaking and will honour the life of the deceased person is all that is required. We would be honoured to contact a Celebrant that meets your needs.
Do we really need a celebrant? Can’t a family member or friend just do that?
No, it is not required to have a Celebrant for your funeral service. Should you want a Celebrant, we would be honoured to arrange for that. The Celebrant will offer your family a very personalized yet structured service based around your loved one with the information you provide to them and can also act as an M.C.
You could also have a family member or friend officiate the service.
Why does the family need to provide music?
Families need to provide recorded music, because of copyright issues. As well, there can be so many versions of the same song, and this way they have the right version sung by the correct artist of their choice.
Should the family desire to have musicians present, we are happy to arrange for an organist, pianist, soloist, violinist, piper, harpist, etc.
Is it a legal requirement to have an obituary?
No it is not a legal requirement to place an obituary, however it is strongly recommended. An obituary provides an opportunity for friends and acquaintances to become informed of the death and allows them to make plans to attend the funeral service or offer condolences to the family member(s) that they know.
I have never had to write an obituary. Can you help me with this?
We do not expect our families to compose the obituary notices for their loved ones.
When the Funeral Director meets with the family we will ask for some biographical information such as, the names and relationship of the surviving family members, and names of those they are predeceased by. We ask for the families to supply this information to us in point form and we will compose the notice for you. Once we have done this, we have the family proof read it and have us make any changes you desire.
You can also visit our Obituary Writing Assistant tool, which is a great way to start a very personalized and thoughtful obituary for your loved one.
How do I place a newspaper notice in those papers?
We will not send the obituary to the newspaper until you are 100% satisfied with it. Let us know which communities the obituary is to appear and we will notify and email them the notice on your behalf.
Can family be pallbearers?
Family members can be pallbearers. As well we can also arrange for professional pallbearers if the family so wishes.
Can we have the reception prior to going to the cemetery?
Yes you can have the reception prior to going to the cemetery. We refer to that as a delayed graveside.
How can I create a memorial for a loved one?
A memorial is the creation of a visible and permanent place or marker to recognize and honor the life of one who has died. Remembering the life of a loved one through a memorial tribute can provide important support and closure for family and loved ones.
The choices for memorials are wide and varied. Some ideas for unique memorials include:
having a stained glass window added to a church to recognize a loved one
donating a park bench to a city park and having it inscribed with your loved one’s name
creating a memorial home-page on the Internet or world-wide-web
planting a tree in either Calgary’s Fish Creek Memorial Forest or in Nose Creek Valley Memorial Forest, or in Airdrie’s Fletcher Park Memorial Forest. (to visit our Tree Program section click here)
placing a grave marker in the cemetery (check the marker requirements with each cemetery)
For those who have chosen cremation, many options exist for memorials surrounding the cremated remains:
an urn can be purchased for burial or placement in an above-ground columbarium
create a special memorial vessel to hold the cremated remains, such as a necklace or bracelet
Whatever permanent memorial selected, these unique reminders are a source of comfort for families and friends, because they are something to return to for generations to come.
How does a funeral director help with the grief process?
The primary role of a funeral director is to assist family and friends with both the practical and emotional side of coping with the loss of a loved one.
Over a few short days, funeral directors handle an estimated two to three hundred activities, requiring about 40-to-45 hours to arrange. Funeral directors are experienced in all legal, medical, cultural and religious procedures to provide the family with caring, individual counsel, and to ensure the funeral is as stress-free and meaningful as it can be.
Funeral directors are also aware of special services – such as financial benefits available to veteran’s families, widows or persons with limited resources – and can help families access this information easily. Some funeral homes also offer service referrals for individuals needing help dealing with loss in the months or years that follow.
All funeral directors in Alberta (Canada) are graduates of a regulated, professional college program. Upon successful completion of a combination of education and on-the-job training, each funeral director is licensed, and continuing education is a post-graduate requirement to maintain their licence.
If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), Click here to send us an e-mail.
Are there differences between funeral homes?
As with most services, there is a great variety of funeral services available to you, in a wide range of prices. To compare funeral homes, the best approach is to make inquiries before a death occurs, or get referrals from a trusted friend or family member.
Some considerations are whether the funeral home is familiar with different ethnic cultures or customs as part of the funeral service, and whether they have the special equipment or rooms set aside to meet these requests.
Many families need a place to meet after the service, but not all funeral homes have reception rooms with catering facilities right on location.
It may be important to you to know whether the funeral home is family-owned and operated, or part of a larger national organization.
Some funeral homes offer special services like personalized service folders, unique memorials such as tree plantings, and traditional white limousines.
Most funeral homes will gladly answer these and other questions, and provide estimates by phone or mail to your home, without any obligation.
If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), Click here to send us an e-mail.
What is important when selecting a funeral home?
Think about what will make the ceremony unique, personal, and meaningful to the family. Then, use these guidelines to find a funeral home that can accommodate your requests, since all have different services and facilities available.
Ask the following questions of the funeral home – they should answer this information without obligation.
Has the funeral home been in business a long time in your city?
Is the funeral home locally owned, or part of a larger national organization?
Are they involved in local community organizations or activities?
Do they have a good reputation for meeting the needs of families?
Is their geographic location convenient and is their building handicap accessible?
Can they provide all services required at their own location?
Do they have small and large chapels to accomodate different size groups?
Do they offer special services for ethnic cultures, and have an excellent understanding of cultural customs and traditions?
Do they offer unique monument ideas, such as special tree planting memorial?
These are just some of the questions to ask when selecting a funeral home. It’s important to choose a licensed funeral home with a good reputation, whom you feel comfortable with.
If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), Click here to send us an e-mail.
When death is expected, what do I do?
When a death is expected, there are a couple of considerations for immediate and future care:
Is medical care needed for the individual?
If so, alternatives include general hospital palliative care units; auxiliary hospitals; provincial and private nursing homes; hospices; or in-home nursing care.
This time can be used to plan or make funeral arrangements. Sometimes, this is difficult for the person involved, so a family member may be asked to make arrangements once death has occurred. If possible, try to discuss preferences beforehand.
Discuss the location of originals for all important business and personal documents, and make a list (and photocopies) so they are easily accessible when they are needed.
When caring for a dying person, make sure you take care of yourself and/or your family’s emotional needs.
Share your experiences with other family members or close friends
Allow friends to help with small tasks, or by giving you time off
If you belong to a church or synagogue, talk to the clergy for spiritual support
Don’t try to get through this time alone – even a little support can help
If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), Click here to send us an e-mail.
What should I do when a death occurs?
If death is sudden or unexpected, call 9-1-1 to notify the police and the coroner’s office. If death was expected, and the deceased was under the care of a physician or health care nurse, then a call to 9-1-1 is not required. A call to your local funeral home should be made as soon as you can.
There are many decisions to be made after the passing of a loved one, and funeral directors are experienced in helping families with this process. Ask a trusted friend or family member to recommend a funeral home they know.
An appointment will be made to discuss arrangements and details, like:
Have advanced plannings been made by the deceased?
What type of service is preferred: burial, cremation, or mausoleum?
Has a cemetery been chosen?
Other personal information about the deceased to register the death with the local government.
The funeral director will also help you select a casket, music, floral tributes, custom stationery, an officiate for the ceremony, and can help write the newspaper notice if desired.
All details will be arranged with utmost care to ensure the service is a personal reflection of the life of the deceased, honoring their unique contribution and meeting the needs of the surviving members of the family.
If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), send us an email. 
What is opening and closing, and why are there fees for it?
Opening and closing fees can include up to and beyond 50 separate services provided by the cemetery. Typically, the opening and closing fees include administration and permanent record keeping (determining ownership, obtaining permission, and the completion of other documentation which may be required, entering the interment particulars in the interment register, maintaining all legal files), opening and closing the grave (locating the grave and laying out the boundaries, excavating and filling the interment space), installation and removal of the lowering device, placement and removal of artificial grass dressing and coco-matting at the grave site, leveling, tamping, re-grading and sodding the grave site, and leveling and re-sodding the grave if the earth settles. 
Can we dig our own grave to avoid the charge for opening and closing?
The actual opening and closing of the grave is just one component of the opening and closing fee. Due to safety issues which arise around the use of machinery on cemetery property, and the protection of other gravesites, the actual opening and closing of the grave is conducted by cemetery grounds personnel only.
Why is having a place to visit so important?
To remember, and to be remembered. A permanent memorial in a cemetery provides a focal point for remembrance and memorializing the deceased. Memorialization of the dead is a key component in almost every culture. Psychologists say that remembrance practices serve an important emotional function for survivors by helping them bring closure, which allows the healing process to begin. The provision of a permanent resting place is an important part of this process.
What happens when a cemetery runs out of land?
When a cemetery runs out of land, it will continue to operate and serve the community. Most cemeteries have crematoriums, and some historic cemeteries even offer guided tours.
How soon after a death must an individual be buried?
The timing depends on the family’s wishes, religious or cultural traditions, and any logistical considerations. Services can take place within days or be delayed several months if needed to allow time for family travel, planning, or special requests.
If a service is held before the burial, this is often referred to as a delayed graveside or committal. Our team will work closely with the family to arrange a timeline that feels right for them and meets all necessary requirements.
Does a body have to be embalmed before it is buried?
No. Embalming is generally a choice, one which depends on factors like if there is to be an open casket viewing of the body, or if there will be an extended time between death and internment. Public health laws may require embalming if the body is going to be transported by air or rail.
What options are available besides ground burial?
These may include cremation, entombment in a mausoleum, or interment in a niche or columbarium. Families may also choose to hold a memorial service without burial, or to place cremated remains at a later date.
What are burial vaults and grave liners?
Most large, active cemeteries have regulations that require the use of a basic grave liner for maintenance and safety purposes. Either a grave liner or a burial vault will satisfy these requirements. Some smaller rural or churchyard cemeteries do not require use of a container to surround the casket in the grave.
There are alternatives to burial. See Cremation Services

How does a funeral director help with the grief process?

The primary role of a funeral director is to assist family and friends with both the practical and emotional side of coping with the loss of a loved one.

Over a few short days, funeral directors handle an estimated two to three hundred activities, requiring about 40-to-45 hours to arrange. Funeral directors are experienced in all legal, medical, cultural and religious procedures to provide the family with caring, individual counsel, and to ensure the funeral is as stress-free and meaningful as it can be.

Funeral directors are also aware of special services – such as financial benefits available to veteran’s families, widows or persons with limited resources – and can help families access this information easily. Some funeral homes also offer service referrals for individuals needing help dealing with loss in the months or years that follow.

All funeral directors in Alberta (Canada) are graduates of a regulated, professional college program. Upon successful completion of a combination of education and on-the-job training, each funeral director is licensed, and continuing education is a post-graduate requirement to maintain their licence.

If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), [Click here to send us an e-mail](mailto:info@mcinnisandholloway.com).

Are there differences between funeral homes?

As with most services, there is a great variety of funeral services available to you, in a wide range of prices. To compare funeral homes, the best approach is to make inquiries before a death occurs, or get referrals from a trusted friend or family member.

Some considerations are whether the funeral home is familiar with different ethnic cultures or customs as part of the funeral service, and whether they have the special equipment or rooms set aside to meet these requests.

Many families need a place to meet after the service, but not all funeral homes have reception rooms with catering facilities right on location.

It may be important to you to know whether the funeral home is family-owned and operated, or part of a larger national organization.

Some funeral homes offer special services like personalized service folders, unique memorials such as tree plantings, and traditional white limousines.

Most funeral homes will gladly answer these and other questions, and provide estimates by phone or mail to your home, without any obligation.

If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), [Click here to send us an e-mail](mailto:info@mcinnisandholloway.com).

What is important when selecting a funeral home?

Think about what will make the ceremony unique, personal, and meaningful to the family. Then, use these guidelines to find a funeral home that can accommodate your requests, since all have different services and facilities available.

Ask the following questions of the funeral home – they should answer this information without obligation.

*   Has the funeral home been in business a long time in your city?
*   Is the funeral home locally owned, or part of a larger national organization?
*   Are they involved in local community organizations or activities?
*   Do they have a good reputation for meeting the needs of families?
*   Is their geographic location convenient and is their building handicap accessible?
*   Can they provide all services required at their own location?
*   Do they have small and large chapels to accomodate different size groups?
*   Do they offer special services for ethnic cultures, and have an excellent understanding of cultural customs and traditions?
*   Do they offer unique monument ideas, such as special tree planting memorial?

These are just some of the questions to ask when selecting a funeral home. It’s important to choose a licensed funeral home with a good reputation, whom you feel comfortable with.

If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), [Click here to send us an e-mail](mailto:info@mcinnisandholloway.com).

When death is expected, what do I do?

When a death is expected, there are a couple of considerations for immediate and future care:

*   Is medical care needed for the individual?
*   If so, alternatives include general hospital palliative care units; auxiliary hospitals; provincial and private nursing homes; hospices; or in-home nursing care.

This time can be used to plan or make funeral arrangements. Sometimes, this is difficult for the person involved, so a family member may be asked to make arrangements once death has occurred. If possible, try to discuss preferences beforehand.

Discuss the location of originals for all important business and personal documents, and make a list (and photocopies) so they are easily accessible when they are needed.

When caring for a dying person, make sure you take care of yourself and/or your family’s emotional needs.

*   Share your experiences with other family members or close friends
*   Allow friends to help with small tasks, or by giving you time off
*   If you belong to a church or synagogue, talk to the clergy for spiritual support
*   Don’t try to get through this time alone – even a little support can help

If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), [Click here to send us an e-mail](mailto:info@mcinnisandholloway.com).

What should I do when a death occurs?

If death is sudden or unexpected, call 9-1-1 to notify the police and the coroner’s office. If death was expected, and the deceased was under the care of a physician or health care nurse, then a call to 9-1-1 is not required. A call to your local funeral home should be made as soon as you can.

There are many decisions to be made after the passing of a loved one, and funeral directors are experienced in helping families with this process. Ask a trusted friend or family member to recommend a funeral home they know.

An appointment will be made to discuss arrangements and details, like:

*   Have advanced plannings been made by the deceased?
*   What type of service is preferred: burial, cremation, or mausoleum?
*   Has a cemetery been chosen?
*   Other personal information about the deceased to register the death with the local government.

The funeral director will also help you select a casket, music, floral tributes, custom stationery, an officiate for the ceremony, and can help write the newspaper notice if desired.

All details will be arranged with utmost care to ensure the service is a personal reflection of the life of the deceased, honoring their unique contribution and meeting the needs of the surviving members of the family.

If you have a question you would like answered by one of our funeral directors (at no obligation), [send us an email](mailto:info@mcinnisandholloway.com). 

What is opening and closing, and why are there fees for it?

Opening and closing fees can include up to and beyond 50 separate services provided by the cemetery. Typically, the opening and closing fees include administration and permanent record keeping (determining ownership, obtaining permission, and the completion of other documentation which may be required, entering the interment particulars in the interment register, maintaining all legal files), opening and closing the grave (locating the grave and laying out the boundaries, excavating and filling the interment space), installation and removal of the lowering device, placement and removal of artificial grass dressing and coco-matting at the grave site, leveling, tamping, re-grading and sodding the grave site, and leveling and re-sodding the grave if the earth settles.   

Can we dig our own grave to avoid the charge for opening and closing?

The actual opening and closing of the grave is just one component of the opening and closing fee. Due to safety issues which arise around the use of machinery on cemetery property, and the protection of other gravesites, the actual opening and closing of the grave is conducted by cemetery grounds personnel only.

Why is having a place to visit so important?

To remember, and to be remembered. A permanent memorial in a cemetery provides a focal point for remembrance and memorializing the deceased. Memorialization of the dead is a key component in almost every culture. Psychologists say that remembrance practices serve an important emotional function for survivors by helping them bring closure, which allows the healing process to begin. The provision of a permanent resting place is an important part of this process.

What happens when a cemetery runs out of land?

When a cemetery runs out of land, it will continue to operate and serve the community. Most cemeteries have crematoriums, and some historic cemeteries even offer guided tours.

How soon after a death must an individual be buried?

The timing depends on the family’s wishes, religious or cultural traditions, and any logistical considerations. Services can take place within days or be delayed several months if needed to allow time for family travel, planning, or special requests.  
If a service is held before the burial, this is often referred to as a delayed graveside or committal. Our team will work closely with the family to arrange a timeline that feels right for them and meets all necessary requirements.

Does a body have to be embalmed before it is buried?

No. Embalming is generally a choice, one which depends on factors like if there is to be an open casket viewing of the body, or if there will be an extended time between death and internment. Public health laws may require embalming if the body is going to be transported by air or rail.

What options are available besides ground burial?

These may include cremation, entombment in a mausoleum, or interment in a niche or columbarium. Families may also choose to hold a memorial service without burial, or to place cremated remains at a later date.  

What are burial vaults and grave liners?

Most large, active cemeteries have regulations that require the use of a basic grave liner for maintenance and safety purposes. Either a grave liner or a burial vault will satisfy these requirements. Some smaller rural or churchyard cemeteries do not require use of a container to surround the casket in the grave.

There are alternatives to burial. See Cremation Services
